newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rexrodt-tax deal must cut burden by over 10 bln dm.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt-tax deal must cut burden by over 10 bln dm.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said that even a watered down tax reform must cut the tax burden by more than 10 billion marks and that he sees chances for a deal with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
"If the SPD really means it seriously we can talk about almost everything," Rexrodt was quoted as telling Bild newspaper in an interview published on Tuesday.
"The decisive point is that the entire tax rate must be reduced, from the bottom to the top tax rate."

The SPD has given a guarded welcome to new scaled-down tax reform proposals floated by the German government as leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition pulled back from an original plan to slash 30 billion marks in income and corporate taxes.

News weekly Der Spiegel said in its edition published on Monday that Finance Minister Theo Waigel was now working on plans to cut the top rate of income tax to 48 or 49 percent from 53 percent. He had originally planned to slash the top tax bracket to 39 percent.
The entry rate of income tax would fall to 22 or 23 percent from 25.9 percent, compared to the 15 percent earlier envisaged.
Rexrodt said: "There must be a net easing (of the tax burden). We can discuss the size. But it must be a double-digit billion-mark figure."

The government's original tax reform package foundered on opposition from the SPD, which controls the Bundesrat (upper house of parliament) and which said the plans were unfair to people on lower incomes.
Rexrodt called on the SPD to end what he called its "blockade" in parliament.
"We want a compromise, but not a rotten one. If the SPD wants to turn our big tax reform into a small redistribution exercise we have to say no."
